name: Aaron Sawit
description: Aaron Sawit is a security engineer in Singapore. He builds free learning tools for students and teachers, runs his own infrastructure, and is good at explaining hard things simply.
about: I work in cybersecurity full time, on the risk and compliance side. I also tutor special needs kids, and have since 2020. That's why the Versed tools exist and why they're free: my students needed calmer, simpler tools than the ones schools pay for, so I built them.

Most of my training has been hands-on. I hold the GIAC Certified Incident Handler and worked through Hack The Box's SOC analyst path. My favourite part of any investigation is when a vague "it's broken" turns into one specific line in one specific log.
Six years of teaching kids who struggle with reading has made me good at something most engineers dodge: explaining a hard thing to someone who isn't technical, without talking down to them.

also.name: pdf-redaction-check
also.what: Checks whether redacted text in a PDF is really gone. It finds words still under black boxes, overlays included, and redaction marks nobody applied. Rewritten after a real document got past my first version.

also.name: llm-guardrail-tests
also.what: Regression tests for the guardrails on your own AI feature: 20 known prompt-injection patterns, graded deterministically with random markers and a canary instead of a judge model. Drops into CI.

also.name: model-diff-audit
also.what: Compares an AI model bit by bit against the base it claims to come from, and tells normal fine-tuning apart from tampering. On a real tampered model, it found the 90 edited rows out of 151,936.

also.name: toolcall-probe
also.what: Asks a local model endpoint straight out whether it really calls tools or just talks about calling them, and tells you which layer is to blame.

also.name: cctokens
also.what: Shows where your Claude Code tokens go: usage and API-equivalent cost by day, model and project. One Python file, no dependencies, nothing leaves your machine. Counts each message once, unlike the logs.

also.name: docker-gpu-reload-check
also.what: Finds containers that will quietly lose their NVIDIA GPU on the next systemd reload, and prints the fix. Read-only. Tested on my own two-GPU server.

also.name: private-relay-block
also.what: Gets Apple devices back behind the network's DNS filter by blocking iCloud Private Relay the way Apple documents it, plus the cached relay addresses. Has a dry run and a clean undo.

also.name: disc-image-id
also.what: Tells Xbox, PS1 and PS2 disc images apart by their signature instead of the file extension, and converts the full Xbox dumps the xemu emulator refuses. Tested and open source.

also.name: Exam-practice tutoring app
also.what: A primary school English app for students and teachers, built with a partner who owns the backend. Hints fade as a student gets the hang of it, and teachers see every attempt. Still in development.

fit.title: Detection and response
fit.text: I do log analysis, SIEM work and incident handling. I write detections other people can read and test, and I keep digging until I can name the one thing that caused it.

fit.title: Security-minded infrastructure
fit.text: I run Linux, containers, networking and monitoring as code, with backups I've actually restored from and a threat model I can explain.

fit.title: Shipping secure products
fit.text: I take products from a blank page to real users on Cloudflare's edge, and I sort out privacy and abuse as part of the design, not as a patch later.

seeking: Security engineering, detection engineering and platform security roles

cv.summary: Security engineer with a First Class computer science degree and the GCIH. By day I assess technology risk against government security policy. I also build and test AI systems: a marking system measured against human examiners, open-source guardrail tests, and a suite of free learning tools used by students. Six years of tutoring special needs students taught me to explain hard things simply.
skills: Third-party and SaaS security risk assessment, policy deviation review, compensating controls, government ICT security policy (IM8), NIST CSF, ISO 27001
LLM applications on AWS Bedrock and Cloudflare Workers AI, prompt evaluation against human marking, prompt-injection regression tests, model file integrity checks, cost and rate caps in code
Sigma rules mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, Elastic Stack and Splunk, Sysmon and Windows event logs, incident handling (SANS SEC504), Wireshark, Nmap, YARA, Snort
AWS Bedrock and IAM, Cloudflare Workers, Durable Objects, D1, KV and Pages, TypeScript, authentication and sessions, rate limiting, CSP and security headers
Linux, Docker and Compose, systemd, iptables, WireGuard and Tailscale, DNS filtering, backups and monitoring

experience.title: Cybersecurity Engineer
points: Assess the security risk of SaaS and third-party services that government agencies want to adopt, against government ICT security policy (IM8).
Review requests to deviate from policy: weigh the risk, check the compensating controls, and recommend whether to approve, reject or change them.
Point of contact for agencies' security policy questions. I turn policy text into a clear answer that engineers can act on.

experience.title: AI Engineer (assignment)
points: Rebuilt an early prototype into a working AI marking system for the group's bootcamp selection exam: Python, Claude on AWS Bedrock (3.5 Sonnet, later Sonnet 4), versioned prompt templates, and parallel marking of a full intake from a spreadsheet.
Wrote the evaluation harness that scores the model against instructor marking, and used it to drive every prompt change: agreement rose from about 60% to about 77%.
Used it on past papers and live applicants, several hundred scripts in all.

experience.title: Cybersecurity Specialist
points: Full-time blue team and red team training programme (the Alpha Specialist Training Bootcamp).
Earned the GIAC Certified Incident Handler (GCIH) through SANS SEC504 and completed the Hack The Box SOC Analyst path.

experience.title: Private Tutor
points: One-to-one tutoring for primary and lower-secondary special needs students, referred by a specialist from the Dyslexia Association of Singapore. The reason the Versed tools exist: I build what my own students need and keep it free.
